description:
Command Line Partitioning


You'll be using fdisk to accomplish this. Lets first find-out list of devices available on our system with command fdisk -l 
Disk /dev/xvdb: 6442 MB, 6442450944 bytes                                        
255 heads, 63 sectors/track, 783 cylinders                                       
...
Disk /dev/xvdc: 4294 MB, 4294967296 bytes                                        
255 heads, 63 sectors/track, 522 cylinders                                       
...                                                                                 
Disk /dev/xvde: 8589 MB, 8589934592 bytes                                        
255 heads, 63 sectors/track, 1044 cylinders
As you can see we have 3 drives where /dev/xvde is our root partition already in use. For illustration, I'll use /dev/xvdb which has around 6GB, and assume that you want a single partition on the disk, occupying all the free space.

1) Initiate fdisk with the following command:

sudo fdisk /dev/xvdb

and type m for help. 
 Command (m for help): m

2) Fdisk will display the following menu: 
   Command action
   a   toggle a bootable flag
   b   edit bsd disklabel
   c   toggle the dos compatibility flag
   d   delete a partition
   l   list known partition types
   m   print this menu
   n   add a new partition
   o   create a new empty DOS partition table
   p   print the partition table
   q   quit without saving changes
   s   create a new empty Sun disklabel
   t   change a partition's system id
   u   change display/entry units
   v   verify the partition table
   w   write table to disk and exit
   x   extra functionality (experts only)
  Command (m for help):

3) We want to add a new partition. Type n and press enter. 
  Command action
   e   extended
   p   primary partition (1-4)

4) We want a primary partition. Enter p and enter. 
  Partition number (1-4):

5) Since this will be the only partition on the drive, number 1. Enter 1 and enter.
If it asks about the first cylinder, just type 1 and enter. (We are making 1 partition to use the whole disk, so it should start at the beginning.) For Last cylinder just press enter again to use entire partition. 
First cylinder (1-783, default 1): 1                                             
Last cylinder, +cylinders or +size{K,M,G} (1-783, default 783):                  
Using default value 783

6) Now that the partition is entered, choose option w to write the partition table to the disk. Type w and enter.

The partition table has been altered!

7) If all went well, you now have a properly partitioned hard drive that's ready to be formatted. Since this is the first partition, Linux will recognize it as /dev/xvdb1, while the disk that the partition is on is still /dev/xvdb
You can view this partition with command like fdisk -l
name: Partition The Disk

description:
To format the new partition as ext3 file system (most stable file-system):

sudo mkfs -t ext3 /dev/xvdb1
If you want recent file system say ext4, substitute ext3 with ext4 in above command.
If everything goes well, you see a output like

name: Format the Drive

description:
When formatting the drive as ext2/ext3, 5% of the drive's total space is reserved for the super-user (root) so that the operating system can still write to the disk even if it is full. However, for disks that only contain data, this is not necessary.

You can adjust the percentage of reserved space with the tune2fs command, like this:

sudo tune2fs -m 1 /dev/xvdb1
This example reserves 1% of space - change this number if you wish.

(i) Using this command does not change any existing data on the drive. You can use it on a drive which already contains data.
name: Modify Reserved Space (Optional)

description:
Now that the drive is partitioned and formatted, you need to choose a mount point. This will be the location from which you will access the drive in the future. I would recommend using a mount point with /mnt. For this example, we'll use the path /mnt/mynewdrive

sudo mkdir /mnt/mynewdrive
Now we are ready to mount the drive to the mount point.
name: Create A Mount Point

description:
Alternatively, you may want to manually mount the drive every time you need it.

For manual mounting, use the following command:

sudo mount /dev/xvdb1 /mnt/mynewdrive
When you are finished with the drive, you can unmount it using:

sudo umount /mnt/mynewdrive

verify the mount point with simple df -h 
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on                                 
/dev/xvde       7.9G  4.4G  3.2G  59% /                                          
tmpfs           296M     0  296M   0% /dev/shm                                   
/dev/xvdb1      6.0G  141M  5.8G   3% /mnt/newdrive
That's it Smile :)

name: Manually Mount

description:
You can choose to have the drive mounted automatically each time you boot the computer, or manually only when you need to use it.
To mount automatically during boot, You'll need to edit /etc/fstab:
sudo nano -Bw /etc/fstab
Add this line to the end (for ext3 file system):
  /dev/xvdb1    /mnt/mynewdrive   ext3    defaults     0        2

where defaults tells system to use default options: rw, suid, dev, exec, auto, nouser, and async and The "2" at the end instructs your system to run a quick file system check on the hard drive at every boot. Changing it to "0" will skip this. Run man fstab for more info here.You can now run
sudo mount -a"
(or reboot the computer) to have the changes take effect.
name: Automatic Mount At Boot

description:
So far we created primary partition. Did you notice, when did "Partition the Disk" prompted for something like 
 Partition number (1-4):

It has numbers up to 4. Whats that mean? It means we can create only upto 4 Primary partition. If we need more than 4 partition, how to create? Again, re-collect during "Partition the Disk" topic, we asked for whether you need 
  Command action
   e   extended
   p   primary partition (1-4)

See "extended" ? Thats our way to create more partitions.
We will see how to create 2 partitions from drive /dev/xvdc which as 4GB in total.
At the end of this session, we will have two partitions named /dev/xvdc5 and /dev/xvdc6
Step 1) Lets start
fdisk /dev/xvdc
Step 2) We choose e for extended partition. 
Command (m for help): n
Command action
   e   extended
   p   primary partition (1-4)

e

Step 3) Provide number for this extended partition. 
Partition number (1-4): 1

Step 4) Press enter twice to keep the default value for extended partition
First cylinder (1-522, default 1):  
Using default value 1
Last cylinder, +cylinders or +size{K,M,G} (1-522, default 522):  
Using default value 522

Step 5) Okay now we have extended partition, now the real work starts, we again do create n for new partiton. 

Command (m for help): n
Command action
   l   logical (5 or over)
   p   primary partition (1-4)
l
See magically now l appears for logical partition instead of e!
Step 6) Choose default for starting cylinder and provide required size for last cylinder , here its 2GB 
First cylinder (1-522, default 1):  
Using default value 1
Last cylinder, +cylinders or +size{K,M,G} (1-522, default 522): +2G

Step 7) We repeat the same process again ignoring Last Cylinder value too
Command (m for help): n
Command action
   l   logical (5 or over)
   p   primary partition (1-4)
l
First cylinder (263-522, default 263): 
Using default value 263
Last cylinder, +cylinders or +size{K,M,G} (263-522, default 522):  
Using default value 522

Step 8) Now ensure you do w to write this changes to disk 
Command (m for help): w
The partition table has been altered!

Calling ioctl() to re-read partition table.
Syncing disks.

Step 9) Finally view our newly created partitions !
fdisk -l /dev/xvdc 

Disk /dev/xvdc: 4294 MB, 4294967296 bytes
255 heads, 63 sectors/track, 522 cylinders
Units = cylinders of 16065 * 512 = 8225280 bytes
Sector size (logical/physical): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
I/O size (minimum/optimal): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
Disk identifier: 0x18ad18db

    Device Boot      Start         End      Blocks   Id  System
/dev/xvdc1               1         522     4192933+   5  Extended
/dev/xvdc5               1         262     2104452   83  Linux
/dev/xvdc6             263         522     2088418+  83  Linux

Step 10) Format the partitions and mount them for use.
mkfs.ext3 /dev/xvdc5
I'll let you to format the other partition and mount it :)
name: Extra : Logical partitions
